title: الباب الثاني في الاقلام السبعة المشهورة . الفصل الاول من الباب الثاني في القلم السرياني — Hammer: "CHAPTER II. The seven most celebrated old alphabets. SECTION I. The Syrian alphabet, (v. orig. p. 9.)" [English p. 4]

primary.copy: Wellcome Library, London, copy of Joseph Hammer (trans.), Ancient Alphabets and Hieroglyphic Characters Explained (London: W. Bulmer and Co., 1806), digitised for the Internet Archive, item b22039910 (https://archive.org/details/b22039910); rights field: Creative Commons Public Domain Mark
primary.work: Kitāb Shawq al-mustahām fī maʿrifat rumūz al-aqlām, ascribed to Ibn Waḥshiyya, in the Arabic text printed by Joseph Hammer with his English version
primary.date: 1806 (the printing; the imprint of the volume)
primary.locator: Arabic part, printed page 9 (printed "9" and "٩"), Bāb II, faṣl 1; scan leaf 214 (BookReader n213, https://archive.org/details/b22039910/page/n213); Hammer's English cites it as "v. orig. p. 9" (English p. 4)
primary.plate: plates/ibn-wahshiyya/syriac-alphabet/table.png (crop x 470-1890, y 1290-2305 of b22039910_jp2/b22039910_0214.jp2, the item's processed JP2, at full size)

table: The Syriac pen (القلم السرياني), the first of the seven pens the heading calls famous (الاقلام السبعة المشهورة; Hammer: "the seven most celebrated old alphabets"): 22 signs in three rows (9, 8, 5), read right to left, each with an Arabic letter printed beneath it, in abjad order from ا to ت; the six letters ث خ ذ ض ظ غ have no sign in this table. Every label was read from the scan and agrees with the order given here.
conventions: Centre-line strokes with the kit pen (5.5). The print's letters are cursive, made with a pen of thick and thin strokes; the centre of the pen's track is traced, and heavy terminals are not widened. Small closed loops that are the bowls of these letters (hāʾ, fāʾ, qāf), printed at full weight, are drawn as path loops, not as kit rings: they are counters of cursive letters, not the light ring-ends of the charaktêres. Heads printed as solid balls (ḥāʾ, yāʾ, rāʾ) are drawn as dots at their printed size, the solid triangular head of shīn as a small closed triangle filled by the pen. The points of dāl and rāʾ are dots. The forms are not corrected towards any chart of Syriac: they are drawn as printed.
variantsDefault: Compared by the independent checker (2026-10-20) with two other copies of the 1806 printing scanned for the Internet Archive: the Getty Research Institute copy (item ancientalphabets01ibnw, page image n215) and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill copy (item ancientalphabets00ibnw, page image n14), both Arabic p. 9, registered onto the Wellcome master and cut to the same cells. The form of this sign is the same in all three copies. The book prints two more Syriac tables in its last section (Arabic pp. 117 and 118), not traced here.
